text: The optimizer is the piece of classical code that makes a variational loop actually converge to a useful answer instead of wandering randomly. Getting it right is one of the highest-leverage decisions in a hybrid project, because it directly controls how many expensive QPU calls the loop makes.

A quantum cost-function evaluation is slow, expensive, and noisy — a statistical estimate, not an exact value — which rules out several standard classical-optimization choices outright. We'll compare a gradient-based method, the parameter-shift rule, against a gradient-free method, SPSA, and see how stopping conditions double as a direct cost control.

Here's the real circuit those evaluations are running against, from IBM Quantum's documentation. Every single optimizer iteration rebuilds this with new parameters and resubmits it — that resubmission is the cost that's actually at stake.

Now the real comparison. A twenty-parameter circuit using the parameter-shift rule needs forty-one evaluations per iteration — over four thousand across a hundred-iteration run. SPSA needs just two evaluations per iteration, regardless of parameter count — only two hundred total. At real Rigetti Ankaa-3 pricing, that's four thousand nine hundred twenty dollars against two hundred forty. SPSA wins by roughly twenty times here, which is exactly why gradient-free methods dominate in practice once a circuit has more than a handful of parameters.

And this is where that choice gets configured for real — Amazon Braket's hybrid job execution settings, where you set exactly which quantum and classical compute this optimizer-driven loop actually runs on.

Next lesson flips to the other side of the circuit: a QPU doesn't hand you an answer, it hands you a dictionary of counts. Turning that into the number your optimizer actually needs is entirely on you.
